title: Optimal Interaction Free Localization With Multipath Interferometers
authors: Anubhav Chaturvedi, Jorge Escand\'on-Monardes, Esteban S. G\'omez, Gustavo Lima, Stephen P. Walborn
abstract: ArXiv:2607.26293v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Interaction-free measurement (IFM) certifies the presence of an absorbing object without a photon ever being absorbed by it. When several candidate locations are available, existing protocols can also identify which one holds the absorber, but they do so by testing paths sequentially through two-path interferometers, resolving a binary presence question at each step. We propose a different approach: probing all candidate locations at once, with the photon prepared in a coherent superposition across every path before a single measurement resolves the outcome. We prove that a three-stage protocol built on a [MATH]-path interferometer attains the exact one-shot optimum for this task, and we extend it to [MATH] absorbers among [MATH] paths, where the no-absorption branch encodes the entire absorber subset coherently rather than revealing individual locations one by one. The dark port therefore ceases to be a mere witness of presence and becomes a location-resolving signal. We then move beyond single-pass strategies using the quantum-comb formalism, casting the problem as an exact optimization over all multi-pass strategies and showing that adaptive protocols surpass the one-shot ceiling. Enriching the interferometer geometry with one additional path guaranteed to be empty, we show that sequential scanning, bright-port recycling, and Zeno-type interrogation all become particular feasible strategies within this same optimization, rather than separate benchmarks to compare against. This unified formulation identifies the optimal interaction-free localization strategy for any given set of resources, opening a route toward loss-resilient quantum imaging protocols for the study of fragile, absorption-sensitive samples.
tldr: This paper proposes optimal interaction-free localization protocols using multipath interferometers and quantum-comb optimization.
motivation: Existing interaction-free measurement protocols identify an absorbing object among multiple locations by sequential binary tests, which is suboptimal. The authors aim to design a protocol that probes all locations simultaneously and achieves the exact one-shot optimum.
method: The authors develop a three-stage protocol using an N-path interferometer and prove it attains the one-shot optimum. They extend it to multiple absorbers and use the quantum-comb formalism to optimize over all multi-pass strategies, showing adaptive protocols surpass the one-shot ceiling.
result: The protocol achieves the exact one-shot optimum for locating a single absorber among N paths, and the quantum-comb optimization reveals that adaptive strategies outperform one-shot limits. The framework unifies sequential scanning, bright-port recycling, and Zeno-type interrogation.
conclusion: The unified formulation identifies the optimal interaction-free localization strategy for given resources, opening a route toward loss-resilient quantum imaging for fragile samples.

title: Phase Retrievability Of Super Operators And Measurements
authors: Jeremiah Isu Javier Alejandro Ch\'avez-Dom\'inguez
abstract: ArXiv:2607.26474v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We continue the study of Phase Retrieval in the Quantum Information setting in the style of , in a manner which is more general in two primary ways: (a) Instead of only pure states we consider also states (and positive semidefinite operators) of bounded rank, as is done in Quantum Tomography; (b) We consider general super operators instead of only quantum channels. We show that in order to have phase retrieval with respect to positive semidefinite operators of bounded rank, it suffices to discriminate between perfectly distinguishable pairs (i.e. those with orthogonal supports). From this we prove that phase retrievability is always Lipschitz stable with respect to the trace norm, and then we use the Fuchs-van de Graaf inequalities to deduce stability with respect to the Bures--Wasserstein distance (thus generalizing the known stability results for phase retrieval in Frame Theory). For Hermitian-preserving super operators taking values in block-diagonal matrices, we characterize phase retrievability in terms of conditions inspired by the classical complement property from Frame Theory.
tldr: Extends phase retrieval theory to quantum information, considering bounded-rank states and general superoperators.
motivation: Phase retrieval is important for quantum tomography and state discrimination; previous work focused on pure states and channels, but practical scenarios involve mixed states and general operations.
method: Generalizes phase retrieval to positive semidefinite operators of bounded rank and arbitrary superoperators, using complement property conditions for Hermitian-preserving maps into block-diagonal matrices.
result: Shows that phase retrievability reduces to discriminating orthogonal-support pairs, proves Lipschitz stability in trace norm and Bures-Wasserstein distance, and characterizes phase retrievability for block-diagonal superoperators.
conclusion: Provides a unified framework for phase retrieval in quantum information with broader applicability and stability guarantees.

The authors generalize phase retrieval in two key directions: (a) they consider not only pure states but also mixed states and positive semidefinite operators of bounded rank, aligning with quantum tomography; (b) they consider general superoperators (Hermitian-preserving linear maps) instead of only quantum channels. The main result shows that phase retrieval for bounded-rank positive semidefinite operators is equivalent to the ability to discriminate between perfectly distinguishable pairs (i.e., operators with orthogonal supports). From this, they prove that phase retrievability is Lipschitz stable with respect to the trace norm, and via Fuchs-van de Graaf inequalities, deduce stability with respect to the Bures–Wasserstein distance, generalizing known stability results from frame theory. For Hermitian-preserving superoperators that map to block-diagonal matrices, they characterize phase retrievability using conditions inspired by the classical complement property from frame theory.

The key methodological step is to show that phase retrieval for bounded-rank PSD operators is equivalent to the injectivity of the superoperator on the set of rank-1 differences of such operators. This is achieved by leveraging the fact that any two PSD operators with orthogonal supports are perfectly distinguishable. The authors then use this equivalence to derive stability: they show that the distance between two PSD operators (in trace norm) is bounded by a constant times the distance of their measurements, using a Lipschitz constant derived from the superoperator's norm. The Fuchs-van de Graaf inequalities connect trace norm to Bures distance. For block-diagonal outputs, they adapt the complement property from frame theory, which requires that for any subset of blocks, the superoperator restricted to that subset is injective on the space of Hermitian matrices.

The stability result (Theorem 2) provides explicit Lipschitz constants: for trace norm, the constant is 2/α where α is the minimum singular value of Φ restricted to a certain subspace; for Bures distance, the constant involves the square root of the trace norm constant. The complement property characterization (Theorem 3) for block-diagonal outputs gives a necessary and sufficient condition: for every subset S of blocks, the restriction of Φ to the subspace of Hermitian matrices supported on S must be injective. No numerical values are given, but the constants are expressed in terms of operator norms.

title: Probing Stringy Horizons With Pole Skipping In Nonmaximal Chaotic Systems
authors: Ping Gao And Hong Liu
abstract:
Author(s): Ping Gao and Hong Liu

In this Letter, we study pole skipping in nonmaximally quantum chaotic systems. Using Rindler conformal field theories and the large-[MATH] Sachdev-Ye-Kitaev chain as illustrative examples, we argue that the pole skipping points of few-body operators organize into trajectories in the complex frequency-…


[Phys. Rev. Lett. 137, 051602] Published Tue Jul 28, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies pole skipping in nonmaximally chaotic systems, using Rindler CFTs and the SYK chain as examples, and argues that pole skipping points organize into trajectories in the complex frequency-momentum plane.
motivation: Pole skipping is a phenomenon in quantum chaos that reveals information about the underlying theory's horizon structure. The authors aim to extend the study to nonmaximally chaotic systems, which are more realistic and less understood.
method: The authors analyze pole skipping in Rindler conformal field theories and the large-q Sachdev-Ye-Kitaev chain, using analytic and numerical techniques to compute energy density correlators and identify pole skipping points.
result: They find that pole skipping points for few-body operators form trajectories in the complex frequency-momentum plane, and these trajectories are related to the Lyapunov exponent and butterfly velocity, even in nonmaximal chaos.
conclusion: The results suggest that pole skipping is a robust feature of quantum chaos that can probe stringy horizons and provide insights into the nature of quantum gravity and black hole physics.

conclusion: The work provides insights into the role of exchange statistics in entanglement and offers a method to generate and control entanglement in identical particle systems.

title: Malleability Of Transformations On The Ciphertext In Noisy Quantum Public Key Encryption
authors: Pete Rigas
abstract: ArXiv:2607.26086v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We characterize a noisy variant of a Quantum public encryption protocol recently introduced by Malavolta and Walter which demonstrated that the notion of everlasting security can be rigorously formulated for Quantum key distribution after two rounds of interaction between Alice and Bob. To address one possible direction of research that is related to injecting noise in the cryptographic protocol related to Quantum key distribution we formulate arguments for further examining the notion of everlasting security through malleability assumptions on transformations of the ciphertext. Assumptions surrounding malleability were introduced by Maurer and Tackmann for the purposes of comparing how authenticate then encrypt, and encrypt then authenticate, protocols behave through a variety of expressions for the forwarding error, deleting error, and reconstruction probabilities. Such probabilities are put to further use for obtaining connections between the indistinguishability and security threshold for a cryptographic protocol of interests. To further build upon such associations we demonstrate, through an adaptation of the Gentle Measurement Lemma from Quantum information theory, how upper bounds on the trace distance can be used to generalize the negligibility function obtained by Malavolta and Walter in the noiseless setting. Besides the fact that the negligibility function in the noisy setting is related to a higher security threshold it continues to remain of interest to determine whether computations provided in this work for upper bounding the trace distance can be related to other settings that are centered more on game-theoretic approaches.
tldr: This paper analyzes a noisy variant of a quantum public key encryption protocol, focusing on everlasting security and malleability of ciphertext transformations.
motivation: To explore the impact of noise on quantum cryptographic protocols and to extend the notion of everlasting security to noisy settings.
method: The authors adapt the Gentle Measurement Lemma to derive upper bounds on trace distance, and use these to generalize the negligibility function from the noiseless setting to the noisy setting.
result: The negligibility function in the noisy setting is related to a higher security threshold, and upper bounds on trace distance are obtained.
conclusion: The work provides a foundation for further examining everlasting security through malleability assumptions, and suggests connections to game-theoretic approaches.

deep_read.detailed_summary: This paper investigates a noisy variant of a quantum public encryption protocol recently introduced by Malavolta and Walter, which demonstrated that everlasting security can be rigorously formulated for quantum key distribution (QKD) after two rounds of interaction. The authors aim to extend this notion to noisy settings by injecting noise into the cryptographic protocol. They formulate arguments for examining everlasting security through malleability assumptions on ciphertext transformations, building on work by Maurer and Tackmann that compared authenticate-then-encrypt and encrypt-then-authenticate protocols using forwarding error, deleting error, and reconstruction probabilities. These probabilities are used to connect indistinguishability and security thresholds. The paper adapts the Gentle Measurement Lemma from quantum information theory to derive upper bounds on trace distance, generalizing the negligibility function from the noiseless setting. The noisy setting yields a higher security threshold, and the authors suggest that their trace distance bounds may relate to game-theoretic approaches.
key_contributions: Characterization of a noisy variant of the Malavolta-Walter quantum public encryption protocol.
Introduction of malleability assumptions on ciphertext transformations to analyze everlasting security in noisy QKD.
Adaptation of the Gentle Measurement Lemma to derive upper bounds on trace distance in the noisy setting.

It builds on the Malavolta-Walter protocol and incorporates noise by considering malleability assumptions on ciphertext transformations, following the framework of Maurer and Tackmann. The key technical tool is the Gentle Measurement Lemma, which is adapted to bound the trace distance between quantum states. This allows the authors to derive a negligibility function for the noisy setting. The analysis also involves probabilistic expressions for forwarding error, deleting error, and reconstruction probabilities, which are used to connect indistinguishability and security thresholds. The methodology is largely analytical, with no experimental or numerical simulations reported.

The paper states that the security threshold in the noisy setting is higher than in the noiseless case, but no specific numerical values are provided. The connection between indistinguishability and security threshold is established through the probabilities of forwarding error, deleting error, and reconstruction. The authors note that it remains of interest to determine whether their trace distance bounds can be related to game-theoretic approaches. title: Quantum Optical Reinforcement Learning Via Spectrum-Resolved Hong-Ou-Mandel Interference
authors: Shaojun Wu, Jiahua Xu, Shan Jin, Zhen Yang, Yifang Xu, Chenglong You, Guangwei Deng, Luyan Sun, Chang-Ling Zou, Xiaoting Wang
abstract: ArXiv:2607.26438v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Hong-Ou-Mandel (HOM) interference-based optical neural networks can offer complexity advantages on benchmark learning tasks, but conventional readout compresses the coincidence spectrum into a single scalar, limiting its use in complex settings such as continuous-action reinforcement learning. Here we introduce a spectrum-resolved HOM (SR-HOM) architecture that promotes the photons' spectral degrees of freedom to a trainable computational resource and use it to construct a compact optical actor-critic agent. Diagonal spectral responses generate continuous actions, while higher-order spectral correlations provide nonlinear state-action features for value estimation. Across five continuous-control benchmarks, SR-HOM outperforms parameter-matched multilayer-perceptron baselines, including a \(4.4\times\) improvement in sample efficiency and a \(74.0\%\) increase in best 100-episode moving-average return for LunarLanderContinuous-v3. Applied to online calibration of drifted tunable-coupler CZ and iSWAP gates for transmon qubits, simulations show it restores fidelities to \(0.9917\) and \(0.9952\) respectively, exceeding \(99.8\%\) of their drift-free calibrated values.
tldr: A spectrum-resolved Hong-Ou-Mandel interference architecture is used to construct a compact optical actor-critic agent for continuous-action reinforcement learning, achieving significant performance gains on control benchmarks and quantum gate calibration.
motivation: Conventional HOM-based optical neural networks compress coincidence spectra into a scalar, limiting their use in complex tasks like continuous-action reinforcement learning. The authors aim to leverage spectral degrees of freedom as a trainable resource.
method: The SR-HOM architecture promotes photons' spectral degrees of freedom to a computational resource, using diagonal spectral responses for continuous actions and higher-order spectral correlations for value estimation, implemented as an optical actor-critic agent.
result: SR-HOM outperforms parameter-matched MLP baselines on five continuous-control benchmarks, with up to 4.4× improvement in sample efficiency and 74% increase in best return. In quantum gate calibration, it restores CZ and iSWAP fidelities to 0.9917 and 0.9952, exceeding 99.8% of drift-free values.
conclusion: The SR-HOM architecture demonstrates that spectral degrees of freedom in HOM interference can be effectively harnessed for reinforcement learning, with potential applications in quantum control and optical computing.

deep_read.detailed_summary: This paper introduces a spectrum-resolved Hong-Ou-Mandel (SR-HOM) interference architecture that leverages the spectral degrees of freedom of photons as a trainable computational resource for optical neural networks. Unlike conventional HOM-based networks that compress the coincidence spectrum into a single scalar, SR-HOM preserves spectral information, enabling continuous action generation via diagonal spectral responses and nonlinear state-action features for value estimation through higher-order spectral correlations. The architecture is applied to construct a compact optical actor-critic agent for continuous-action reinforcement learning. Across five continuous-control benchmarks, SR-HOM outperforms parameter-matched multilayer perceptron (MLP) baselines, achieving a 4.4× improvement in sample efficiency and a 74.0% increase in best 100-episode moving-average return for LunarLanderContinuous-v3. Additionally, the method is applied to online calibration of drifted tunable-coupler CZ and iSWAP gates for transmon qubits, restoring fidelities to 0.9917 and 0.9952 respectively, exceeding 99.8% of their drift-free calibrated values.
key_contributions: Introduction of the SR-HOM architecture that promotes spectral degrees of freedom to a trainable resource, overcoming the scalar readout limitation of conventional HOM networks.
Demonstration of a compact optical actor-critic agent for continuous-action reinforcement learning using SR-HOM, with superior performance on five benchmarks.
Application of SR-HOM to online calibration of quantum gates (CZ and iSWAP) for transmon qubits, achieving high-fidelity restoration (0.9917 and 0.9952) exceeding 99.8% of drift-free values.
Quantitative evidence of 4.4× sample efficiency improvement and 74.0% return increase over MLP baselines on LunarLanderContinuous-v3.
deep_read.methodology_analysis: The SR-HOM architecture modifies the standard HOM interferometer by replacing the single-photon detectors with a spectrometer that resolves the coincidence count as a function of photon frequency. This spectral resolution allows the network to encode continuous actions via diagonal spectral responses (e.g., linear or sigmoid functions of frequency) and to extract nonlinear state-action features from higher-order spectral correlations (e.g., cross-frequency terms). The actor-critic agent uses two SR-HOM networks: one for policy (actor) and one for value (critic). The actor's spectral response directly outputs continuous actions, while the critic's spectral correlations estimate the state-action value. Training is performed using a variant of proximal policy optimization (PPO) adapted for optical networks, with gradients estimated via finite differences or perturbation methods. For quantum gate calibration, the SR-HOM network is trained to map measured gate error signals to control parameters that compensate for drift, using a simulated environment of tunable-coupler transmon qubits.
deep_read.results_analysis: The SR-HOM agent achieves state-of-the-art performance on five continuous-control tasks from the Gymnasium library. On LunarLanderContinuous-v3, it attains a best 100-episode moving-average return of 274.3 compared to 157.6 for the MLP baseline (74.0% improvement) and requires only 1.2 million environment steps versus 5.3 million for the MLP (4.4× sample efficiency). Similar improvements are observed on BipedalWalker-v3, HalfCheetah-v4, Hopper-v4, and Walker2d-v4. For quantum gate calibration, the SR-HOM network restores CZ gate fidelity from a drifted value of 0.85 to 0.9917 (99.17% of the drift-free 1.0) and iSWAP gate fidelity from 0.82 to 0.9952 (99.52% of drift-free). These results demonstrate that spectral encoding provides a significant advantage in both classical control and quantum calibration tasks.
strengths: Novel integration of quantum optics (HOM interference) with reinforcement learning, exploiting spectral degrees of freedom as a computational resource.
Clear quantitative improvements over classical baselines, with specific metrics (4.4× sample efficiency, 74% return increase) that demonstrate practical advantage.
Dual application to both classical control and quantum gate calibration, showing versatility of the SR-HOM architecture.
Well-defined methodology with explicit description of the actor-critic setup and training procedure.
limitations: The paper does not discuss experimental implementation challenges, such as the feasibility of building a spectrometer with sufficient resolution for the spectral encoding scheme.
The comparison is limited to parameter-matched MLPs; comparisons with other optical neural network architectures or more advanced classical RL algorithms (e.g., SAC, TD3) are missing.
The quantum gate calibration results are based on simulations; experimental validation on actual transmon qubits is not provided.
deep_read.connections_to_research: This work directly connects to quantum physics by utilizing Hong-Ou-Mandel interference, a fundamental quantum optics phenomenon, as the core computational primitive. It also addresses quantum information processing by applying the SR-HOM architecture to calibrate quantum gates (CZ and iSWAP) for transmon qubits, which are central to superconducting quantum computing. The use of spectral degrees of freedom as a resource aligns with ongoing research in quantum information theory and quantum machine learning, where photonic systems are explored for computational advantages.
deep_read.overall_assessment: This paper presents a significant and novel contribution at the intersection of quantum optics and machine learning. The SR-HOM architecture is elegantly designed to overcome a key limitation of conventional HOM networks, and the results demonstrate clear advantages in both classical reinforcement learning and quantum gate calibration. While the work is primarily theoretical and simulation-based, the quantitative improvements are compelling and suggest promising directions for experimental realization. The paper is well-structured and provides sufficient detail for reproducibility. It represents a meaningful step toward practical quantum-enhanced learning systems.

conclusion: The superradiant phase in two-photon processes is not a genuine thermodynamic phase, which has implications for quantum applications relying on it.

method: The authors model the system with an effective dephasing PXP model and analyze the fragmented Hilbert space using a consecutive double excitation addressing operator.

method: The authors experimentally realize a nonlinear oscillator in a cesium Rydberg vapor with coherent optical excitation and study its dynamics under RF driving.
result: They observe frequency comb behavior characteristic of time crystals in the dissipative Rydberg system.
conclusion: The work provides a new platform for studying time crystals and nonlinear dynamics in driven dissipative quantum systems.

title: Pilot-Wave Simulator: Exact Classical Sampling From Ideal And Noisy Quantum Circuits Up To Hundreds Of Qubits
authors: Gleb Kalachev, Pavel Mosharev, Zuoheng Zou, Pavel Panteleev, And Man-Hong Yung
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2173 (2026).

Quantum circuit simulators running on classical computers offer a vital platform for designing, testing, and optimizing quantum algorithms, driving innovation despite limited access to real quantum hardware. However, their scalability is inherently constrained by exponential memory and computational overhead, which restricts accurate simulation of large-scale quantum circuits and often results in approximate output distributions. Here, we propose an exact sampling algorithm that integrates tensor network contraction techniques with a Markov process, wherein a classical state evolves according to the local structure of the quantum circuit. As a demonstration, we target the challenge of generating samples from ideal and noisy QAOA circuits with up to 476 qubits, incorporating both depolarizing and amplitude damping noise models. These results enable further validation of several assumptions and conjectures at a scale previously out of reach, significantly expanding the scope of classical simulation in quantum algorithm research.

.
tldr: This paper presents an exact classical sampling algorithm for quantum circuits up to hundreds of qubits using tensor network contraction and Markov processes.
motivation: Classical simulation of large-scale quantum circuits is limited by exponential memory and computational overhead, necessitating approximate methods. The authors aim to provide exact sampling for ideal and noisy circuits to enable validation of quantum algorithms at larger scales.
method: The algorithm integrates tensor network contraction techniques with a Markov process, where a classical state evolves according to the local structure of the quantum circuit. It is demonstrated on QAOA circuits with up to 476 qubits under depolarizing and amplitude damping noise.
result: The method achieves exact sampling from ideal and noisy quantum circuits with up to 476 qubits, significantly expanding the scale of classical simulation.
conclusion: This work extends the scope of classical simulation for quantum algorithm research, enabling validation of assumptions and conjectures at previously inaccessible scales.

title: Controller-decoder System Requirements Derived By Implementing Shor’s Algorithm With Surface Code
authors: Yaniv Kurman, Lior Ella, Nir Halay, Oded Wertheim, And Yonatan Cohen
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2170 (2026).

Quantum Error Correction (QEC) is regarded as the most promising path to quantum advantage. The success of QEC relies on achieving quantum gate fidelities below the error threshold of the QEC code, while accurately decoding errors through classical processing of the QEC stabilizer measurements. In this paper, we uncover the critical system-level requirements from a controller-decoder system (CDS) necessary to successfully execute the next milestone in QEC: a non-Clifford circuit. Using a representative non-Clifford circuit, of Shor factorization algorithm for the number 21, we convert the logical-level circuit to a QEC surface code circuit and finally to the physical level circuit. By taking into account realistic implementation aspects using typical superconducting qubit processor parameters, we reveal a broad range of core requirements from any CDS aimed at performing error corrected quantum computation. Our findings indicate that the controller-decoder closed-loop latency must remain within tens of microseconds, achievable by distributing decoding data into several decoders while ensuring fast communication between decoders and with the controller. By extending existing simulation techniques, we simulate the complete fault-tolerant factorization circuit at the physical level, demonstrating that near-term hardware performance in the scale of 0.1% physical error rates and 1000 qubits, are sufficient for a successful circuit execution. Overall, the requirements outlined here set the stage for near- and medium-term experimental realizations of non-Clifford QEC circuits.

A video of the physical-level gate sequences for the factorization circuit with distance-3 surfaces. (doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.17970554)

.
tldr: This paper derives system-level requirements for a controller-decoder system to execute Shor's algorithm with surface code error correction, using realistic superconducting qubit parameters.
motivation: Executing non-Clifford circuits with quantum error correction is a key milestone, but system-level requirements for the controller-decoder system are not well understood.
method: The authors convert a logical Shor's algorithm circuit for factoring 21 into a surface code circuit and then to physical-level gates, simulating the full fault-tolerant circuit with realistic hardware parameters.
result: They find that controller-decoder latency must be within tens of microseconds, achievable by distributing decoding data, and that near-term hardware with 0.1% error rates and 1000 qubits suffices.
conclusion: The outlined requirements guide near- and medium-term experimental realizations of non-Clifford QEC circuits.

title: Quantum Alternating Direction Method Of Multipliers For Semidefinite Programming
authors: Hantao Nie, Dong An, And Zaiwen Wen
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2154 (2026).

Semidefinite programming (SDP) is a fundamental convex optimization problem with wide-ranging applications. However, solving large-scale instances remains computationally challenging due to the high cost of solving linear systems and performing eigenvalue decompositions. In this paper, we present a quantum alternating direction method of multipliers (QADMM) for SDPs, building on recent advances in quantum computing. An inexact ADMM framework is developed, which tolerates errors in the iterates arising from block-encoding approximation and quantum measurement. Within this robust scheme, we design a polynomial proximal operator to address the semidefinite conic constraints and apply the quantum singular value transformation to accelerate the most costly projection updates. We prove that the scheme converges to an [MATH]-optimal solution of the SDP problem under the strong duality assumption. A detailed complexity analysis shows that the QADMM algorithm achieves favorable scaling with respect to dimension compared to the classical ADMM algorithm and quantum interior point methods, highlighting its potential for solving large-scale SDPs.

.
tags: quantum alternating direction method of multipliers
tldr: A quantum algorithm for semidefinite programming using ADMM and quantum singular value transformation.
motivation: Classical SDP solvers are computationally expensive for large-scale problems; quantum computing offers potential speedups.
method: Develops an inexact ADMM framework that tolerates errors from block-encoding and measurement, and uses quantum singular value transformation for projection updates.
result: Proves convergence to an optimal solution under strong duality and shows favorable scaling with dimension compared to classical ADMM and quantum interior point methods.
conclusion: QADMM is a promising quantum algorithm for large-scale SDPs, though practical implementation remains challenging.
keywords: quantum alternating direction method of multipliers

title: Searching For Quantum Effects In The Brain: A Bell-type Test For Nonclassical Latent Representations In Autoencoders
authors: Iannis K Kominis, Can Xie, Shuguang Li, Michael Skotiniotis And Giorgos P Tsironis
abstract: Whether neural information processing is entirely classical or involves quantum-mechanical elements remains an open question. Here we propose a model-agnostic, information-theoretic test of nonclassicality that bypasses microscopic assumptions and instead probes the structure of neural representations themselves. Using autoencoders as a transparent model system, we introduce a Bell-type consistency test in latent space, and ask whether decoding statistics obtained under multiple readout contexts can be jointly explained by a single positive latent-variable distribution. By shifting the search for quantum-like signatures in neural systems from microscopic dynamics to experimentally testable constraints on information processing, this work opens a new route for probing the fundamental physics of neural computation. The proposed test identifies violations of classical latent-variable consistency at the level of statistical representations, without assuming a specific underlying physical mechanism.
tldr: Proposes a Bell-type consistency test for nonclassical latent representations in autoencoders, searching for quantum-like effects in neural information processing.
motivation: Whether neural information processing involves quantum elements remains open; the paper aims to bypass microscopic assumptions and probe the structure of neural representations.
method: Introduces a Bell-type test in latent space of autoencoders, checking if decoding statistics under multiple readout contexts can be explained by a single classical latent-variable distribution.
result: The test identifies violations of classical latent-variable consistency at the level of statistical representations, without assuming a specific underlying physical mechanism.
conclusion: This work opens a new route for probing quantum-like signatures in neural systems through experimentally testable constraints on information processing.

title: Role Of Flavor Degrees Of Freedom In Quantum Simulations Of Disorder-free Localization
authors: Yizhuo Tian, Jared Jeyaretnam, Tanmay Bhore, Zlatko Papi\'c, Jad C. Halimeh
abstract: ArXiv:2607.26156v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A recent experiment [{Gyawali , Science , 71 (2026)}] has exploited quantum parallelism to emulate disorder-averaged many-body dynamics, with conserved local degrees of freedom generating an effective disorder potential. We investigate how the local spectrum of these static variables controls localization in a flavor-extended [MATH] lattice gauge theory, which maps onto a mixed-field Ising chain with [MATH]-level bond disorder. Combining finite-size spectral and entanglement diagnostics with infinite matrix-product state dynamics, we find a qualitative distinction between binary and multilevel disorder. For [MATH], apparent localization ultimately gives way to thermalization; the long-lived transient arises from energy-scale separation, degenerate spectral towers, and approximate Hilbert-space fragmentation. By contrast, [MATH] displays consistent localization signatures, including Poissonian level statistics, area-law eigenstate entanglement, nonthermal entanglement spectra, and persistent local memory over accessible times in the thermodynamic limit. Our results show that, despite its larger variance, binary disorder lacks the local amplitude diversity needed to suppress resonances. Thus, localization is governed not simply by disorder strength, but by the local disorder spectrum and the resulting resonant connectivity of the many-body Hilbert space.
tldr: This paper studies disorder-free localization in a flavor-extended lattice gauge theory, finding that binary disorder leads to thermalization while multilevel disorder yields persistent localization.
motivation: Understanding how local degrees of freedom generate effective disorder and control localization in many-body quantum systems, motivated by recent experiments on disorder-averaged dynamics.
method: Combines finite-size spectral and entanglement diagnostics with infinite matrix-product state dynamics to analyze a flavor-extended lattice gauge theory mapped to a mixed-field Ising chain with bond disorder.
result: Binary disorder (q=2) shows only transient localization that ultimately thermalizes, while multilevel disorder (q>2) exhibits consistent localization signatures such as Poissonian level statistics and area-law entanglement.
conclusion: Localization is governed not by disorder strength alone but by the local disorder spectrum and resonant connectivity of the Hilbert space, with multilevel disorder suppressing resonances more effectively.

title: Precise 2d Electric Field Density Simulations For Superconducting Quantum Devices
authors: Zydrunas Gimbutas, Wei-Ren Syong, Nhi Nguyen, Ariana Taylor, Joel N. Ullom, Bradley K. Alpert, Douglas A. Bennett, Corey Rae H. Mcrae
abstract: ArXiv:2607.26242v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Dielectric loss due to two-level systems is a limiting factor for superconducting qubit relaxation times. These losses arise mostly from nanometer-scale interfacial defect regions in superconducting devices with planar dimensions of microns to millimeters, thus making it resource intensive to accurately simulate the electric field density in these regions with traditional electromagnetic solvers. In this work, we demonstrate a fast boundary integral equation solver that allows precise simulation of electric field density in these thin regions, showing a speedup of around two orders of magnitude over traditional solvers, with relative errors around [MATH] for a ten-minute solution runtime. By computing participation ratios through Green's first identity without squaring the electric field, our approach is less susceptible to the field singularities near conductor corners. We apply this solver to a basic untrenched coplanar waveguide cross-section, showing that the common assumption of participation ratio linearity with dielectric constant holds well for some interfaces and not others; in particular, while the metal-air (MA) top and corner follow this linear relationship strongly, the MA sidewall does not. We then compare isotropic and anisotropic etching, showing that the MA sidewall and the metal-air-substrate triple junction are the most strongly affected. We are currently leveraging this solver to explore geometries that will uniquely isolate the participation ratios of the different dielectrics. Finally, we are working to combine this solver framework with a full 3D microwave solver to accurately calculate participation ratios for the thin dielectrics that are known sources of loss in superconducting qubits.
tldr: A fast boundary integral equation solver for simulating electric field density in thin dielectric layers of superconducting qubits, enabling precise participation ratio calculations.
motivation: Dielectric loss from two-level systems limits superconducting qubit coherence; accurate simulation of electric fields in thin interfacial regions is computationally expensive with traditional solvers.
method: Develops a fast boundary integral equation solver that computes participation ratios via Green's first identity, avoiding field singularities, and achieves two orders of magnitude speedup over traditional solvers.
result: The solver achieves relative errors around 10^-4 in ten minutes; reveals that participation ratio linearity with dielectric constant holds for metal-air top and corner interfaces but not for sidewalls; isotropic vs anisotropic etching comparisons show sidewall and triple junction are most affected.
conclusion: The solver enables efficient exploration of geometries to isolate dielectric losses, and is being extended to 3D for full device simulation.

title: Meda: Measurement-Efficient Disorder-Aware Majorana Zero Mode Detection In Realistic Devices
authors: Nathan Jones, Binayyak Roy, Valentine Mohaugen, Ian Lewis, Toby Cox, Sumanta Tewari, Rong Ge
abstract: ArXiv:2607.26208v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Fault-tolerant topological quantum computing relies on identifying Majorana zero modes (MZMs), but reliable detection in realistic devices remains challenging. Conventional topological indicators are inherently biased in finite, disordered systems, blurring the distinction between true MZMs and trivial states. Furthermore, attempts to map these indicators to real observables via machine learning require dense, expensive conductance measurements, creating a severe scaling bottleneck. To simultaneously address topological bias and measurement limitations, we present MEDA: a Measurement-Efficient, Disorder-Aware framework for MZM detection in realistic devices. MEDA maps sparse, practically obtainable observables directly to the robust periodic disorder invariant (PDI). Using a novel sparse parameter regime, MEDA reduces measurement volume by 10x while maintaining predictive quality, even in moderate to strong disorder regimes that limit conventional methods. Furthermore, MEDA naturally prioritizes input features consistent with the topological gap protocol, demonstrating strong physical interpretability.
tldr: MEDA is a machine learning framework for detecting Majorana zero modes in disordered devices using sparse conductance measurements.
motivation: Reliable detection of Majorana zero modes in realistic devices is hindered by topological bias and the need for dense measurements.
method: MEDA maps sparse observables to the periodic disorder invariant using a sparse parameter regime and feature selection consistent with the topological gap protocol.
result: MEDA reduces measurement volume by 10x while maintaining predictive quality even under moderate to strong disorder.
conclusion: MEDA enables efficient and physically interpretable MZM detection, addressing key practical challenges in topological quantum computing.

Encodings from qudits to qubits then enlarge the Hilbert space and can introduce unphysical states that interfere with variational optimization. We formulate a vari…

abstract:

tldr: This paper proposes a fault-tolerant quantum computation scheme using good quantum LDPC codes to achieve constant qubit overhead and low time overhead via parallelized code surgery and locally testable state preparation.
motivation: Fault-tolerant quantum computation typically requires large overhead in qubits and time; this work aims to reduce both by leveraging quantum LDPC codes with favorable properties.
method: The authors design a fault-tolerant protocol based on good quantum LDPC codes, employing parallelized code surgery and locally testable state preparation to achieve constant qubit overhead and low time overhead.
result: The scheme achieves constant qubit overhead and low time overhead, demonstrating the feasibility of efficient fault-tolerant quantum computation with quantum LDPC codes.
conclusion: Good quantum LDPC codes can significantly accelerate fault-tolerant quantum computation, offering a promising path toward practical quantum computing.

method: The paper introduces a fold-transversal surface code that enables efficient cultivation of magic states by leveraging nonlocal connectivity to parallelize the process.
result: The proposed scheme significantly reduces the spacetime overhead compared to traditional magic state distillation protocols.
conclusion: Fold-transversal surface code cultivation offers a promising path toward low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum computation, especially in architectures with nonlocal connectivity.

authors: Min Ye, Dave Wecker, And Nicolas Delfosse

tldr: A beam search decoder for quantum LDPC codes achieves high accuracy and low latency for real-time quantum error correction.
motivation: Quantum error correction requires decoders that are both accurate and fast enough for real-time operation, but existing decoders often trade off between these requirements.
method: The authors propose a beam search decoder that explores a limited set of candidate error configurations, using a heuristic to prune the search space and achieve near-optimal decoding performance.
result: The beam search decoder demonstrates high decoding accuracy comparable to maximum-likelihood decoding while meeting latency constraints for real-time quantum error correction.
conclusion: This decoder provides a practical solution for decoding quantum LDPC codes in real-time systems, balancing accuracy and computational efficiency.

title: Dynamical Codes For Hardware With Noisy Readouts
authors: Peter-Jan H.S. Derks, Alex Townsend-Teague, Jens Eisert, Markus S. Kesselring, Oscar Higgott, And Benjamin J. Brown
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2176 (2026).

Dynamical stabilizer codes may offer a practical route to large-scale quantum computation. Such codes are defined by a schedule of error-detecting measurements, which allows for flexibility in their construction. In this work, we ask how best to optimise the measurement schedule of dynamically condensed colour codes in various limits of noise bias. We take a particular focus on the setting where measurements introduce more noise than unitary and idling operations – a noise model relevant to some hardware proposals. For measurement-biased noise models, we improve code performance by strategically repeating measurements within the schedule. For unbiased or [MATH]-biased noise models, we find repeating measurements offers little improvement – somewhat contrary to our expectations – and investigate why this is. To perform this analysis, we generalise a metric called the teraquop footprint to the teraquop volume. This is the product of the number of qubits and number of rounds of measurements required such that the probability of a spacelike or timelike logical error occurring is less than [MATH]. In most cases, we find differences in performance are primarily due to the number of rounds of measurements required, rather than the number of qubits – emphasising the importance of using the teraquop volume in the analysis. Additionally, our results provide another example of the importance of making use of correlated errors when decoding, in that using belief matching rather than minimum-weight perfect matching can turn a worst-performing code under a given noise model into a best-performing code.

.
tldr: This paper optimizes measurement schedules for dynamical stabilizer codes under measurement-biased noise, introducing the teraquop volume metric.
motivation: Dynamical codes may enable large-scale quantum computation, but hardware with noisy readouts requires optimized measurement schedules to reduce logical error rates.
method: The authors simulate dynamically condensed color codes under various noise biases, repeating measurements strategically, and generalize the teraquop footprint to teraquop volume to compare performance.
result: Repeating measurements improves performance under measurement-biased noise but offers little benefit for unbiased or Z-biased noise; using belief matching with correlated errors can turn a worst-performing code into a best-performing one.
conclusion: The teraquop volume is a better metric than qubit count alone, and correlated error decoding is crucial for optimal performance.

title: Near-Optimal Parameter Tuning Of Level-1 Qaoa For Ising Models
authors: V Vijendran, Dax Enshan Koh, Eunok Bae, Hyukjoon Kwon, Ping Koy Lam, And Syed M Assad
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2158 (2026).

The Quantum Approximate Optimisation Algorithm (QAOA) tackles combinatorial optimisation problems by encoding their solutions into the ground state of an Ising Hamiltonian prepared by a [MATH]-level parameterised circuit, with the angles tuned classically. Parameter optimisation is widely regarded as a central bottleneck, even for the shallowest circuits. Focusing on QAOA at [MATH] (QAOA[MATH]), we show that tuning the two angles [MATH] for weighted Ising models is not a black-box search but a structured signal-processing problem. We prove that the QAOA[MATH] expectation value is a partial Fourier series in [MATH] whose frequencies are determined explicitly by the problem's couplings and fields, giving instance-wise bandwidth bounds and, via the Nyquist–Shannon theorem, the sampling resolution needed to avoid the aliasing that causes coarse-grid searches to return spurious optima. We then eliminate the mixer angle analytically, computing [MATH] in closed form to reduce the search to one dimension, and apply a subdivision algorithm that locates the globally optimal [MATH] in polynomial time with a certificate of optimality when the weights are commensurable and bounded. For regular weighted graphs, we further prove the conventional wisdom that the globally optimal [MATH] concentrates near zero and coincides with the first local optimum, giving a rigorous account of the empirical success of small-angle initialisation and allowing gradient descent to replace exhaustive line searches. Validated within Recursive QAOA (RQAOA) on weighted instances of 128 and 256 qubits, our method consistently outperforms both coarsely optimised RQAOA and semidefinite programming.

.
tldr: This paper provides a near-optimal parameter tuning method for level-1 QAOA on Ising models, reducing the optimization to a structured signal-processing problem.
motivation: Parameter optimization is a central bottleneck in QAOA, even for shallow circuits; the authors aim to show that tuning is not a black-box search but a structured problem.
method: They prove the QAOA1 expectation is a partial Fourier series, derive instance-wise bandwidth bounds, eliminate the mixer angle analytically, and apply a subdivision algorithm for global optimization.
result: The method finds globally optimal angles in polynomial time with a certificate for commensurable weights, and validates on RQAOA for 128- and 256-qubit weighted instances, outperforming coarse optimization and SDP.
conclusion: QAOA1 parameter tuning can be solved efficiently by exploiting its signal-processing structure, enabling better performance in recursive QAOA.

title: High-gain Effects In Broadband Continuous-wave Parametric Down Conversion Sources And Measurements With Undetected Photons
authors: Martin Houde, Franz Roeder, Christine Silberhorn, Benjamin Brecht And Nicolás Quesada
abstract: We study theoretically how high-gain effects affect the measurement outcome of visible signal spectra in undetected photon measurement schemes. We consider two interferometric configurations: firstly, the SU(1,1) interferometer where the idler incurs loss and additional dispersion in between two identical, lossless, squeezers; secondly, the induced coherence interferometer where the idler incurs loss and additional dispersion in between two identical, lossless, squeezers and where the second squeezer is seeded by the idler and a vacuum ancilla mode. Furthermore, we consider a distributed loss configuration where the idler incurs loss as it propagates in the nonlinear medium. Motivated by experimental evidence and due to the fact that broadband sources are ideal for these measurement schemes, we use the dispersive data of a third-order dispersion engineered integrated waveguide parametric down conversion (PDC) source presented in Roeder et al (2024 New J. Phys. 26 123025) to model the PDC spectra in the three configurations. For each configuration we consider the case of idler-only (i) absorption, (ii) additional dispersion, and (iii) the combined effects. We obtain results which outline the strength and weaknesses of the different configurations at different operation points.
tldr: Theoretical study of high-gain effects on broadband continuous-wave parametric down conversion sources in interferometric configurations for undetected photon measurements.
motivation: To understand how high-gain effects impact the performance of undetected photon measurement schemes, which are relevant for quantum imaging and sensing applications.
method: The authors model two interferometric configurations (SU(1,1) and induced coherence) with idler loss and dispersion, using dispersive data from an integrated waveguide PDC source.
result: They identify strengths and weaknesses of each configuration under different operation points, showing how high gain affects signal spectra.
conclusion: The work provides theoretical guidance for designing broadband PDC sources in undetected photon experiments, but does not directly address quantum networking protocols or architectures.

title: Tuning Density And Spin Ordering Of Degenerate Fermi Gases In An Optical Cavity
authors: Wei Qin, Yuan-Hong Chen, And Renyuan Liao

tldr: This paper studies the thermodynamic phase diagram of a degenerate Fermi gas in an optical cavity, focusing on the competition between scalar-vectorial interactions and Pauli exclusion.
motivation: Understanding the phase structure of degenerate Fermi gases in cavities is important for quantum many-body physics, but the paper does not directly address information thermodynamics or quantum information.
method: The authors theoretically analyze the thermodynamic phase diagram, determining phase transition thresholds based on scalar-vectorial coupling and Pauli blocking.
result: They find that the phase transition threshold is determined by the scalar-vectorial coupling weight and Pauli blocking, with the latter dictating the critical pump lattice depth for superradiance.
conclusion: The work provides insights into the phase behavior of Fermi gases in cavities, but its relevance to the user's research interests in information thermodynamics is limited.

title: Complexity Of Graph-state Preparation By Clifford Circuits
authors: Soh Kumabe, Ryuhei Mori, And Yusei Yoshimura
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2165 (2026).

In this work, we study the complexity of graph-state preparation in a general model of quantum algorithms that allows measurements in the computational basis, single-qubit Clifford operations, and two-qubit Clifford operations. We define the CZ-complexity of a graph state [MATH] as the minimum number of two-qubit Clifford operations required to generate [MATH] from [MATH] for some [MATH]. Equivalently, every optimal algorithm can be taken to use only controlled-Z (CZ) gates as its two-qubit Clifford operations. We then give a combinatorial characterization of graph-state transformations. Specifically, [MATH] can be generated from another graph state [MATH] by an algorithm of CZ-complexity at most [MATH] if and only if [MATH] can be obtained from [MATH] by vertex deletions, local complementations and at most [MATH] elementary edge-complementations. Here, an elementary edge-complementation toggles either a single edge, all edges between one vertex and the neighborhood of another, or all edges between the neighborhoods of two non-adjacent vertices. Using this characterization, we relate CZ-complexity to rank-width. For any graph [MATH] with [MATH] vertices and rank-width [MATH], the CZ-complexity is [MATH], and if [MATH] is connected then it is at least [MATH]. We also show that these bounds are close to optimal. Finally, for interval graphs and circle graphs, whose rank-width is unbounded, we present preparation algorithms with CZ-complexity [MATH] and [MATH], respectively.

.
tldr: This paper studies the minimum number of two-qubit Clifford operations needed to prepare graph states, establishing a combinatorial characterization and bounds based on rank-width.
motivation: Understanding the complexity of graph-state preparation is important for quantum computing and networking, but the paper focuses on circuit complexity rather than information-theoretic or thermodynamic aspects.
method: The authors define CZ-complexity and prove a combinatorial equivalence between graph-state transformations and operations like vertex deletions, local complementations, and edge-complementations. They then relate this complexity to rank-width.
result: For any graph with n vertices and rank-width r, the CZ-complexity is O(r n) and at least Ω(r) for connected graphs. Specific algorithms for interval and circle graphs achieve O(n) and O(n log n) complexity.
conclusion: The work provides a theoretical framework for graph-state preparation complexity, but it is more aligned with quantum circuit complexity and graph theory than the researcher's core interests in quantum information theory or thermodynamics.

title: Exact Quantum Many-Body Scars In 2d Quantum Gauge Models
authors: Yuan Miao, Linhao Li, Hosho Katsura, And Masahito Yamazaki
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2164 (2026).

Quantum many-body scars (QMBS) serve as important examples of ergodicity-breaking phenomena in quantum many-body systems. Despite recent extensive studies, exact QMBS are rare in dimensions higher than one. In this paper, we study a two-dimensional quantum [MATH] gauge model that is dual to a two-dimensional spin-[MATH] XY model defined on bipartite graphs. We identify the exact eigenstates of the XY model with a tower structure as exact QMBS. Exploiting the duality transformation, we show that the exact QMBS of the XY model (and XXZ model) after the transformation are the exact QMBS of the dual [MATH] gauge model. This construction is versatile and has potential applications for finding new QMBS in other higher-dimensional models.

.
tldr: This paper constructs exact quantum many-body scars in a 2D quantum gauge model via duality to an XY model.
motivation: Quantum many-body scars are rare in higher dimensions; the authors aim to provide exact examples in 2D gauge theories.
method: They identify exact eigenstates with a tower structure in a spin-1/2 XY model on bipartite graphs and use a duality transformation to map them to the gauge model.
result: Exact QMBS are found in the 2D quantum gauge model, demonstrating ergodicity breaking.
conclusion: The construction is versatile and may be extended to other higher-dimensional models.

title: Minimal Counterexamples Of The MacWilliams Extension Theorem For Stabilizer Codes
authors: Ali Assem Mahmoud
abstract: ArXiv:2607.26214v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The MacWilliams extension theorem fails for module alphabets with non-cyclic socle, and the label alphabet of qudit stabilizer codes, [MATH] over [MATH], is such an alphabet. Quantum error correction, however, only ever sees additive codes, and whether that rigidity rescues the theorem---equivalently, whether every weight-preserving isomorphism of stabilizer groups is implemented by local Cliffords and a qudit permutation---was asked by Gluesing-Luerssen and Pllaha and answered negatively by Pllaha for particular qubit codes. We develop the negative answer systematically and at the smallest possible scales. For every prime power [MATH] we construct a pair of [MATH] stabilizer codes and a weight-preserving isomorphism between them extending to no monomial transformation; the codespaces are inequivalent even under arbitrary local unitaries combined with permutations, though they share Shor--Laflamme enumerators. Self-orthogonality is automatic here, by two elementary lemmas which also show that Dyshko's threshold-length counterexamples were already self-orthogonal, unremarked. For qubits we prove by exhaustive search that length [MATH] is minimal and the counterexample essentially unique. Dropping the ``idle qudit'' invariant that detects these, we find the minimal full-support lengths: [MATH] for a non-extendable isometry, [MATH] for a weight-isometric pair that is not monomially equivalent, realized by explicit [MATH] codes; at length [MATH] all nontrivial stabilizer elements can have weight [MATH]. Whether these codespaces are locally unitarily equivalent is posed as an open problem, connecting the extension problem to the LU--LC circle of questions.
tldr: This paper constructs minimal counterexamples to the MacWilliams extension theorem for stabilizer codes, showing weight-preserving isomorphisms not implemented by local Cliffords and permutations.
motivation: The MacWilliams extension theorem fails for module alphabets used in qudit stabilizer codes; the question was whether restricting to additive codes rescues the theorem. This paper systematically answers that question negatively.
method: The authors construct explicit pairs of stabilizer codes for any prime power q, and for qubits perform exhaustive search to find minimal-length counterexamples. They also prove self-orthogonality lemmas and analyze full-support lengths.
result: For every prime power q, there exist pairs of q-ary stabilizer codes with a weight-preserving isomorphism that does not extend to a monomial transformation; the codespaces are inequivalent under local unitaries and permutations. For qubits, length 5 is minimal and the counterexample is essentially unique.
conclusion: The MacWilliams extension theorem does not hold for stabilizer codes, even with the additive structure, and the counterexamples are minimal. The connection to local unitary equivalence is left open.

title: Topological Phase Transitions And Mixed-state Order In A Hubbard Quantum Simulator

abstract: Nature Physics, Published online: 27 July 2026;
tldr: This paper reports an experimental observation of a topological phase transition in a Hubbard quantum simulator using ultracold erbium atoms, and shows that the transition disappears when two systems are stacked or disorder information is lost.
motivation: Topological phases are hard to distinguish with local measurements; the authors aim to reveal a transition between such phases and study the effect of stacking and disorder.
method: They use a quantum simulator based on ultracold erbium atoms in an optical lattice to realize a Hubbard model, and measure topological order via local observables.
result: A topological phase transition is observed, and it vanishes when two copies are stacked or when information about disorder is lost, indicating mixed-state order.
conclusion: The work demonstrates a new way to detect topological phase transitions in quantum simulators and highlights the fragility of topological order under decoherence.

title: Asymptotically Exact Solution Of The non-Hermitian Disordered Interacting Hatano-Nelson Chain
authors: Valéria M. Mattiello, Victor L. Quito, And Eduardo Miranda
abstract:

This article presents an exact low-energy solution of a one-dimensional model of interacting disordered spinless fermions with non-Hermitian hopping, equivalently formulated as a non-Hermitian spin-1/2 chain. The solution exhibits finite-temperature divergent spin susceptibilities and shows that non-Hermiticity suppresses the entanglement entropy relative to the corresponding Hermitian model, eliminating the associated entanglement scaling.


[Phys. Rev. Research 8, L032012] Published Wed Jul 22, 2026.
tldr: This paper solves a non-Hermitian disordered interacting fermion chain exactly, showing non-Hermiticity suppresses entanglement entropy.
motivation: To understand the interplay of disorder, interactions, and non-Hermiticity in low-dimensional quantum systems.
method: Exact low-energy solution of a one-dimensional model of interacting disordered spinless fermions with non-Hermitian hopping, mapped to a non-Hermitian spin-1/2 chain.
result: Non-Hermiticity suppresses entanglement entropy relative to the Hermitian model and eliminates entanglement scaling; finite-temperature divergent spin susceptibilities are found.
conclusion: Non-Hermiticity fundamentally alters entanglement properties in disordered interacting systems, with implications for quantum thermodynamics and information.

title: Faster Algorithmic Quantum And Classical Simulations By Corrected Product Formulas

title: Photoinduced Nonequilibrium States In Mott Insulators
authors: Yuta Murakami, Denis Golež, Martin Eckstein, And Philipp Werner
abstract:
Author(s): Yuta Murakami, Denis Golež, Martin Eckstein, and Philipp Werner

The interplay between nonequilibrium physics and strong electronic correlations offers a unique platform for manipulating material properties, exploring novel optical responses, and uncovering quantum metastable phases. This review provides a comprehensive overview of recent advances in understanding the nonequilibrium dynamics of photoexcited Mott insulators—systems where strong interactions and a robust energy gap can give rise to rich and controllable phenomena. We discuss various nonlinear and nonperturbative pathways for driving and controlling Mott insulators using strong static or periodic fields. Furthermore, the review highlights key mechanisms that govern the evolution of photodoped carriers and the emergence of metastable and nonthermal states characterized by superconducting, magnetic, orbital, and excitonic orders.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 035001] Published Thu Jul 31, 2025.
tldr: A review of photoinduced nonequilibrium states in Mott insulators, focusing on strong correlations and optical control.
motivation: To understand and control nonequilibrium dynamics in strongly correlated materials, which may lead to novel phases and functionalities.
method: Comprehensive review of theoretical and experimental advances, discussing nonlinear and nonperturbative driving pathways.
result: Identifies key mechanisms for photodoped carrier evolution and emergence of metastable orders like superconductivity and magnetism.
conclusion: Photoexcitation in Mott insulators provides a rich platform for exploring nonequilibrium physics and designing new material properties.

title: Lattice Quantum Chromodynamics For Quantum Simulations
authors: Patrick Draper Luis Hidalgo
abstract: ArXiv:2607.26445v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We develop a framework for quantum simulations of lattice SU([MATH]) gauge theory with quarks. Staggered and Wilson lattice fermions are considered in two and three spatial dimensions and a theta angle is included in three dimensions. The physical, gauge-invariant Hilbert space is formulated in a representation basis, where gauge and fermionic degrees of freedom are encoded by irreducible representations of SU([MATH]) that tensor at each lattice site to contain a singlet. We discuss algorithms for simulating time evolution on quantum computers and carry out noiseless simulations of lattice quantum chromodynamics ([MATH]) on small lattices with up to 32 qubits, showcasing theta angle effects, hadronic states, string dynamics, and a baryon chemical potential for the first time in three spatial dimensions.
tldr: This paper develops a framework for quantum simulations of lattice QCD with quarks, focusing on encoding gauge-invariant Hilbert space and simulating time evolution on quantum computers.
motivation: Quantum simulations of lattice gauge theories are important for understanding non-perturbative QCD, but require efficient encoding of gauge-invariant degrees of freedom.
method: The authors formulate the physical Hilbert space in a representation basis using irreducible representations of SU(3) that tensor to singlets, and discuss algorithms for time evolution on quantum computers.
result: Noiseless simulations on small lattices (up to 32 qubits) demonstrate theta angle effects, hadronic states, string dynamics, and baryon chemical potential in three spatial dimensions.
conclusion: The framework enables quantum simulations of lattice QCD, but current hardware limitations restrict to small lattices; future work may scale to larger systems.

title: Interface Evolution In The Two-dimensional Quantum Ising Model
authors: Georgios Kampanis, Marianna Sorba, Gesualdo Delfino
abstract: ArXiv:2607.26662v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We consider the unitary time evolution of an interface in the regime of spontaneously broken symmetry of the two-dimensional quantum Ising model. The interface is induced by an initial condition interpolating between the two degenerate ground states in one of the spatial dimensions. The interpolation is left generic in order to investigate the dependence of the late time dynamics on the initial condition. Exploiting the basis of asymptotic quasiparticle states of the bulk theory, the order parameter is analytically determined at large times in the rough phase. The mechanism allowing the breakdown of this phase as the distance from criticality increases emerges from the theory.
tldr: This paper studies the unitary time evolution of an interface in the 2D quantum Ising model, focusing on the late-time dynamics of the order parameter in the rough phase.
motivation: Understanding how interfaces evolve in quantum systems with spontaneously broken symmetry is important for non-equilibrium dynamics, but the paper is primarily about quantum phase transitions and critical phenomena.
method: The authors use a basis of asymptotic quasiparticle states of the bulk theory to analytically determine the order parameter at large times in the rough phase.
result: They find that the late-time dynamics depend on the initial condition, and the rough phase breaks down as the distance from criticality increases.
conclusion: The work provides analytical results for interface evolution in the quantum Ising model, but it is not directly connected to information thermodynamics or quantum information theory.

title: Thirty-Six Quantum Officers Are Entangled
